Keywords: Trade, Art, Brain

outputs.L1:
**Trade—Trade versus Art; Brain—Brain versus Heart!**

Oh, the earthliness of these hard-hearted times,  
When clinking dollars and jingling dimes  
Drown all the finer music of the soul.

Trade, like an octopus, has but this creed:  
That all the world was made to serve his greed.  
He spreads his mighty, myriad claws  
And draws into his foul, polluted maw  
The brightest and the best.

Well-nigh has he drained dry  
The sacred fount of Truth;  
And if, forsooth, he has left  
Some struggling streams to flow,  
He has so contaminated their course  
That Truth is scarcely true.

Poor Art, with struggling gasp,  
Lies strangled, dying in his mighty grasp.  
He locks his grimy fingers  
About her tender, snowy throat.  
Is there no power to rescue her—  
To protect and defend her?

Shall Art be left to perish?  
Shall all the images her shrines cherish  
Be abandoned to this iconoclast—  
To vulgar Trade?

Oh, that mankind had less of Brain  
And more of Heart!  
Oh, that the world had less of Trade  
And more of Art!

Then would there be less grinding down of the poor;  
Then would men learn to love one another more.  
For Trade stalks like a giant through the land,  
Bearing the rich aloft in his high hand,  
While beneath his mighty, ponderous tread  
He crushes those who cry for daily bread.
outputs.L2:
Commerce against beauty, intellect against compassion—  
what a coarse and merciless age this is,  
when the rattle of coins overwhelms  
the soul’s gentler harmonies.

Life has become an octopus ruled by one belief:  
the whole earth exists to satisfy its hunger.  
Commerce reaches everywhere with countless powerful arms,  
dragging nearly everything noble and brilliant  
into its filthy, corrupted mouth.  
It has almost emptied  
the holy spring of Truth;  
and whatever faint currents still escape  
have been so poisoned  
that truth itself is barely truthful anymore.

Impoverished Art, breathless and resisting,  
is suffocating in Commerce’s iron grip.  
His stained hands tighten  
around her delicate white neck.  
Is there no force able to save, shelter, or defend her?  
Must Art be allowed to die?  
Must the treasured figures within her sanctuaries  
be surrendered to this destroyer of sacred images—  
common, crude Commerce?

If only humanity possessed less cold intellect  
and greater feeling;  
if only the world valued business less  
and beauty more.  
The poor would not be oppressed so harshly,  
and people would learn to care more deeply for one another.

For Commerce strides across the country like a colossus,  
raising the wealthy high in one enormous hand,  
while beneath the crushing weight of his steps  
he destroys those pleading merely for enough bread to survive.
outputs.L3:
The poem offers a powerful condemnation of a materialistic age in which money and commerce have come to dominate human life, drowning out the soul’s finer values. Trade is portrayed as a greedy octopus whose tentacles spread through society, consuming its brightest qualities and corrupting even the sacred source of truth. Under this destructive influence, art is strangled and threatened with extinction by the vulgar power of commercial interests.

In response, the speaker urges humanity to reconsider its priorities. Compassion and creativity should be valued more highly than intellect used merely for personal advantage, financial profit, or commercial expansion. The poem also exposes the social injustice caused by unrestrained commerce: while it increases the wealth and power of the privileged, it oppresses and impoverishes those who struggle to obtain even the basic necessities of life. Ultimately, the poem calls for a more humane society—one guided not by greed, but by empathy, imagination, truth, and a genuine concern for human well-being.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a powerful critique of greed and the dehumanizing effects of commerce when the pursuit of profit becomes society’s highest goal. Through striking personification and vivid imagery, Trade is transformed from an ordinary human activity into something monstrous and destructive. It appears like a giant octopus whose tentacles reach into every part of life, seizing people, institutions, and values within its grasp. It is also portrayed as a crushing giant, suggesting that unchecked economic power overwhelms the weak and reduces human beings to objects valued only for their usefulness or financial worth.

Against this threatening force, the poem places truth, art, compassion, and the human heart. These ideals represent everything that cannot be measured in money: honesty, imagination, beauty, sympathy, and love. Yet under the rule of greed, truth is corrupted or silenced whenever it interferes with profit. Art is strangled because creativity is forced to serve commercial interests rather than express genuine feeling or vision. The poor suffer most of all, oppressed by a system that enriches the powerful while ignoring the dignity and needs of vulnerable people.

The poem does not condemn all trade or material prosperity. Instead, it warns against excessive devotion to wealth and the belief that financial gain is more important than human life. When commerce controls morality, culture, and social relationships, it destroys the very qualities that make society humane. The poem therefore urges its readers to resist greed and restore truth, creativity, and compassion to their proper place. Only by valuing people above profit and the heart above wealth can society become more just, loving, and fully human.
outputs.L5:
### The Trade of Ideas

Trade is often described as the exchange of goods, but its deepest currency has always been human imagination. Along ancient routes, merchants carried silk, spices, and precious metals. Yet they also transported stories, symbols, techniques, and beliefs. Every marketplace became a meeting point where unfamiliar ideas could enter the brain and transform the way people understood the world.

Art grew through these encounters. A painter adopted colors from distant lands; a sculptor discovered new forms; musicians combined foreign rhythms with local traditions. What began as trade became cultural invention. Art, in this sense, is not created in isolation. It is shaped by movement, exchange, and the brain’s ability to connect old knowledge with new experiences.

The brain itself is a kind of marketplace. Memories, emotions, and perceptions continually trade information. Creativity emerges when unexpected connections are made—when a practical object inspires a sculpture, when a commercial symbol becomes a painting, or when an ancient pattern appears in modern design.

Trade moves objects, art gives them meaning, and the brain turns exchange into possibility. Together, they reveal that human progress depends not only on what we possess, but also on what we share.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic late-19th-century poem contrasting commerce and art, portraying Trade as a greedy octopus that corrupts truth, strangles beauty, and crushes the poor.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Octopus of Trade**

Beneath the gas-lamps’ jaundiced flare,  
Where midnight looms above the mart,  
A monstrous Kraken coils in air  
And winds its suckers round the heart.  
Its brow is brass, its eyes are gold,  
Its breath the smoke of furnace-fires;  
It counts the young, it buys the old,  
And fattens on the world’s desires.

Men call it Trade. From wharf to throne  
Its glistening tentacles are spread;  
It grinds the orphan’s little bone  
To bleach the rich man’s bridal bed.  
It drags pale Truth before the crowd,  
And decks her out in purchased lies,  
While brokers praise its name aloud  
And fling their ledgers to the skies.

One arm enfolds the judge’s chair,  
One stains the pulpit’s snowy stole;  
One plucks the poet’s garland bare,  
One sets a tariff on the soul.  
It takes fair Beauty by the throat  
And bids her sing a hireling tune;  
Then sells each false, voluptuous note  
Beneath the melancholy moon.

“O Art!” I cried, “arise, arise!  
Bring forth thy sword of living flame!  
Strike through the scales that blind our eyes,  
And brand this swollen Beast with shame!  
Hast thou not stood where empires fell,  
A stainless star above their dust?  
Hast thou not rung the tyrant’s knell  
And taught the broken heart to trust?”

Then Art appeared—a woman wan,  
With violet shadows on her face;  
Her robe was torn, her feet were bare,  
Yet heaven lingered in her grace.  
No jewelled chain adorned her breast,  
No merchant’s seal her brow confined;  
A wild rose trembled at her crest,  
A dawn eternal filled her mind.

She touched the alleys, and they bloomed;  
She kissed the slave, and he was free;  
She sang—and through the factory gloom  
Men heard the immemorial sea.  
But Trade, enraged, its coils uncurled  
And smote her harp with iron hands:  
“Thy song,” it hissed, “must serve the world—  
And I alone command the lands!”

Then from the mills there rose a cry,  
The poor man’s terrible refrain;  
It shook the roofs, it clove the sky,  
It made a sacrament of pain.  
The children, crushed beneath the wheel,  
The mothers starved at plenty’s gate,  
Cried: “Art, make adamant our steel!  
Cry Truth, though Truth should come too late!”

She raised her shattered harp on high;  
One chord across the darkness ran—  
So pure, the stars leaned from the sky,  
So fierce, it woke the soul of Man.  
The Octopus drew back in dread;  
Its golden eyes grew dull as clay:  
For Beauty, strangled, was not dead,  
And Truth, though trampled, faced the day.

O lords who dine while nations weep,  
O merchants throned on human scars,  
Gold cannot buy the dreams that keep  
Their silent vigil with the stars.  
The mart shall sink, the coin shall rust,  
The brazen ledgers cease to be;  
But Art shall rise from blood and dust—  
A flame no chain can bind, or sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a socially critical poem titled “Trade versus Art, Brain versus Heart” in ornate Victorian language.
counterfactuals.output:
# **Trade versus Art, Brain versus Heart**

Beneath the soot-besmirchèd dome of Trade,  
Where iron Mammon counts his clinking gains,  
The pale mechanic, by his loom betrayed,  
Winds golden splendour out of fleshly pains.  
The merchant, throned upon a ledger’s sum,  
Hears not the orphan’s thin, importunate cry;  
His columns speak—the starving streets are dumb—  
And dividends ascend while children die.

There Art, poor seraph, with a tatter’d wing,  
Stands at the gate where brazen Lackeys sneer:  
“What market bears the visions that you bring?  
What price hath Beauty in the fiscal year?”  
She bows her head; her laurel wreath is sere,  
Her lyre lies pawn’d to purchase coals and bread;  
Whilst vulgarest baubles, gaudy and insincere,  
By Fashion crown’d, are royally misread.

O Brain! proud engine of the latter age,  
Thou build’st the bridge, the cannon, and the mart;  
Thou writ’st cold figures on the pauper’s page,  
Yet hast no cipher for a broken heart.  
Thy mills may roar, thy cables gird the foam,  
Thy engines cleave the mountain’s ancient side—  
But what avail, if Want infest the home,  
And man grow mean as mechanism grows wide?

O Heart! thou crimson rebel in the breast,  
Whom prudent lips call foolish, frail, and blind,  
Thou know’st the babe unfed, the maid oppress’d,  
The old man cast like refuse to the wind.  
Thou canst not balance empire’s vast account,  
Nor coin compassion with the statesman’s art;  
Yet one warm tear outweighs the whole amount  
That Brain hath hoarded in his marble chart.

Behold the lord, in perfumed ease reclined,  
Whose mines drink daylight from a thousand men;  
He praises Progress, patronage, and Mind,  
Then bids the footman shut the beggar’s den.  
His walls blaze rich with saints by masters dead,  
His table groans beneath excess and pride;  
He buys Christ painted, framed in burnish’d lead,  
But leaves Christ living famish’d at his side.

Thus Trade weds Brain beneath a gas-lit sky,  
And bells of brass proclaim the contract blest;  
While Art and Heart, like houseless sisters, lie  
Where midnight frost makes marble of the breast.  
Yet from their lips a mightier hymn shall rise  
Than all the anthems Commerce buys with gold:  
For Truth, though scorn’d, hath thunder in her eyes,  
And Love is young when empires have grown old.

Then rend the ledger where it chains the soul;  
Let Science kneel, not reign, beside mankind;  
Let Beauty share the loaf, and Mercy toll  
A nobler summons through the crowded mind.  
Trade is a servant—make it not a throne;  
Brain is a lamp—but Heart must be its flame:  
Else wealth shall glitter over dust and bone,  
And Progress be Oppression’s prouder name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free-verse polemic lamenting how capitalism and materialism drown out the soul, destroy art, deepen poverty, and replace compassion with cold intellect.
counterfactuals.output:
We built a market in the sanctuary  
and taught the bells to ring for profit.

Every silence was leased,  
every horizon branded,  
every hand instructed  
to measure its worth  
by what it could carry away.

The soul spoke softly—  
so we installed louder machines.

They hammered through the night,  
minting hunger into numbers,  
turning forests into receipts,  
turning hours into wages  
too thin to live on,  
turning people into costs  
to be cut.

Art arrived barefoot,  
with paint beneath its nails  
and an impossible song in its mouth.

We asked for its business plan.

We shaved the wildness from its face,  
priced its grief,  
framed its rebellion,  
sold limited editions  
of the fire it came to spread.

Meanwhile, poverty widened  
like a wound beneath a tailored sleeve.

The poor were lectured on discipline  
by those inheriting keys.  
Children learned the arithmetic of absence:  
one meal divided by three,  
one room multiplied by six,  
zero doctors,  
zero mercy,  
interest accruing.

And intellect—  
bright, bloodless instrument—  
was crowned above compassion.

It calculated suffering efficiently,  
called starvation an externality,  
called eviction an adjustment,  
called despair a failure  
of personal investment.

How clean the language became  
as the streets grew crowded.

How elegant the theories  
that never smelled the shelter,  
never held the shaking cup,  
never watched a mother  
choose which need  
would go unanswered.

We were told to be reasonable.

Reasonable as a locked door.  
Reasonable as a ledger  
that balances perfectly  
after the dead are erased.

But the soul is not efficient.

It lingers.  
It forgives without return.  
It makes useless music  
for the lonely.  
It breaks bread  
without asking for proof of hunger.

And art is not a luxury  
dangling above the desperate—  
it is the desperate breathing,  
the buried voice striking the coffin,  
the human animal refusing  
to become inventory.

Listen:

beneath the engines,  
beneath the auctions,  
beneath the endless sermon  
of more,

something unpriced  
is still singing.

Faintly now—  
but not yet gone.

Put your ear to the ruined earth.

It is asking  
not what we own,

but whether,  
after owning everything,

we will remember  
how to feel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Personify Trade as a monstrous giant with many claws and Art as a vulnerable woman in need of rescue. Use rhetorical questions, vivid imagery, and an impassioned archaic tone.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold! Trade reareth his mountainous bulk above the smoke-blackened city—a monstrous giant, iron-crowned, with a hundred grasping claws. One talon rendeth beauty from the loom; another shackleth song to the market-stall; a third scratcheth cold prices upon the very brow of heaven. His breath is furnace-fume, his laughter the clink of coin on coin.

And beneath him standeth Art: pale, unarmoured, yet radiant still, a woman robed in torn colours, clasping one last golden lyre unto her breast. Her hands are bruised; her garland lieth trampled in the mire. Shall none behold her? Shall none arise whilst that many-fingered tyrant draggeth her toward his counting-house? Must every dream be weighed, every melody branded, every vision sold beneath the hammer?

Nay! Awake, ye hearts not wholly turned to stone! Break the giant’s ledgers; strike the fetters from her wrists! Let Trade serve at her threshold, not reign upon her throne. For if Art be devoured, what splendour shall remain to ransom mankind from dust? What song shall comfort the weary? What light shall pierce the long, mercenary night?

Up, then! Rescue her—ere the last bright colour fadeth from the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long poetic passage arguing that the world needs less trade and brain and more art and heart, with references to clinking money, polluted truth, iconoclasm, and the oppression of the poor.
counterfactuals.output:
Let the markets close their iron mouths for an hour.  
Let the ledgers sleep beneath a quiet layer of dust.  
We have listened too long to the clinking of money,  
to coins congratulating coins in marble chambers,  
while outside, the hungry count the windows of bakeries  
and the poor are taught to call their oppression order.

The world has had enough of trade without tenderness,  
of bargains struck across the bent backs of strangers,  
of ships swollen with plenty passing shores of need,  
of hands measuring grain by profit  
while children measure winter by the thinness of their coats.  
Commerce has made a map of every river,  
numbered every forest, priced the marrow of the mountain,  
and asked, with perfect seriousness,  
what the sunset is worth by the acre.

And the brain—bright engine, sleepless accountant—  
has devised a thousand elegant explanations  
for why the table must remain too small,  
why one man’s cup should overflow  
while another drinks the rumor of rain.  
Reason, severed from mercy, becomes a polished knife.  
It can divide the earth into ownership and waste,  
can prove that suffering is efficient,  
can make a prison mathematically sound.  
It can build towers high enough  
that those within no longer hear  
the human voices at their doors.

We do not need less wisdom,  
but less worship of cleverness;  
not less thought, but fewer thoughts  
that have forgotten how to kneel beside grief.  
For truth itself has been polluted—  
smoked over by slogans, poisoned by convenience,  
poured into bright bottles and sold back to us  
with the name of virtue printed on the label.  
The air is thick with manufactured certainty.  
Even lies have learned to wear spectacles,  
to quote statistics, to speak in calm official tones  
while the dispossessed are dragged from their homes.

What we need is art:  
not decoration for the banquet halls of power,  
but the wild red flower breaking through the courthouse steps;  
the song that enters where permission is denied;  
the mural painted on the wall that hid the wounded;  
the poem slipped beneath the factory door  
like bread, like fire, like news of another world.

We need iconoclasm—not the barren joy of smashing,  
but the holy courage to strike the false halo  
from whatever cruelty has called itself sacred.  
Let every idol of profit be questioned.  
Let the golden statues of conquest lose their names.  
Let us break the image that says wealth is goodness,  
that poverty is failure,  
that power is proof of worth.  
Let us shatter the mirror in which empire admires itself,  
and from the pieces make a thousand small windows  
through which the forgotten may be seen.

Give us painters who remember the miner’s lungs,  
musicians who can hear the seamstress coughing at midnight,  
dancers who carry in their bodies  
the weight of fields harvested by underpaid hands.  
Give us sculptors who carve not generals on horseback  
but mothers waiting outside locked hospitals;  
children sleeping beneath advertisements for luxury;  
workers whose names have vanished  
into the products they made.

Give us stories that refuse to flatter the comfortable.  
Give us theaters where the poor are not scenery,  
where their hunger is not a metaphor  
but an accusation with eyes.  
Give us novels that enter the rooms  
where rent is a monthly thunder,  
where every illness is also a debt,  
where hope must be hidden from the landlord  
like a candle from the wind.

Above all, give us heart—  
that ancient, disobedient instrument  
which cannot hear a cry and call it an abstraction.  
The heart does not ask whether compassion is profitable.  
It does not demand a receipt for kindness.  
It knows that a loaf divided is not diminished,  
that shelter is not a prize,  
that no child was born owing tribute  
to the machinery of another’s abundance.

Let the heart return to the council table,  
mud on its shoes, tears on its face.  
Let it interrupt the experts.  
Let it tear open the curtains  
and point toward the streets.  
Let it say: Here is your theory made flesh.  
Here is the cost of your clever arrangement.  
Here is the woman choosing between medicine and heat.  
Here is the man whose labor built the palace  
and whose body is forbidden from its shade.

The world does not need another empire of calculation.  
It needs a chorus.  
It needs hands untrained in counting  
but fluent in holding.  
It needs fewer auctions of the sacred,  
fewer treaties written in invisible ink,  
fewer futures traded by men  
who will not live to endure them.

Let money clink more softly, then,  
until it remembers it is only metal,  
only paper, only a promise we invented—  
not a god, not a judge, not blood.  
Let trade become exchange rather than conquest,  
and intellect become a lantern rather than a throne.  
Let art teach the brain to dream beyond advantage,  
and let the heart teach the world  
that no prosperity is worthy of the name  
if it flowers from the oppression of the poor.

For a civilization is not measured  
by the height of its towers  
or the speed of its transactions,  
but by the tenderness with which it meets the broken;  
by whether beauty is shared like water;  
by whether truth can breathe in the public square;  
by whether the least powerful may stand upright  
without begging permission from the rich.

So let us build no more temples to accumulation.  
Let us build rooms where songs are free.  
Let us trade some portion of our restless brilliance  
for the patient radiance of compassion.  
Let us abandon the cold arithmetic  
that subtracts whole lives from the sum of progress.

Less trade, when trade means chains.  
Less brain, when brain means pride.  
More art, to make the hidden visible.  
More heart, to make the visible beloved.

And when the clinking money falls silent at last,  
may we hear beneath it what was always there:  
the low, persistent music of human need,  
the drum of dignity beneath every rib,  
and the unfinished poem of the world  
asking not to be bought,  
but to be healed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
